results.summary: This design renders 3D scenes to VGA using a per-scanline ray-tracing-derived algorithm and simultaneously plays a 24-voice synthesizer through a PWM audio output with delta-sigma modulation. It is controlled by eight inputs that select speedup, interlace disable, and scene advance, and it outputs standard Tiny VGA signals plus audio on a bidirectional pin. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod and Mike's audio Pmod, and it starts running immediately after reset with all inputs low. It was created for the TTSKY26a demo competition and includes a speedup option that trades PWM resolution and rendering quality for timing margin at the intended 50.4 MHz clock.

This is a side-scrolling runner game where the player jumps or crouches to avoid rocks and birds, with a game over when an obstacle is hit. It is played with a gamepad connected through latch, clock, and data pins, and it outputs VGA video plus PWM audio for background and game-over sounds. It needs a VGA Pmod, a gamepad Pmod, and an audio Pmod to operate. The documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the gameplay and the required external hardware.

This design accepts two 8-bit numbers and produces an approximate 8-bit result, with one input bit selecting between addition and multiplication. It is a purely combinational block with no external hardware required, and its outputs can be wired to LEDs for validation. The documentation is very thin and does not describe the approximation scheme, error characteristics, or any silicon test results. It is notable only as an ASIC implementation of an approximate arithmetic unit.

This design generates a wall-clock-style display on a standard 640x480 at 60 Hz VGA output. It is used by running the clock at 25.2 MHz, connecting a Tiny VGA Pmod, and applying a reset pulse. The only external hardware required is the Tiny VGA Pmod. The documentation is minimal and does not describe the clock face, timekeeping source, or any configuration options.

This design multiplies two 2x2 matrices of signed 8-bit elements into signed 16-bit results using a systolic array of four multiply-add-accumulate processing elements. It is controlled through eight data inputs plus load, transpose, activation, and done signals, with results presented on eight output pins, and it is intended to be driven by an external microcontroller that supplies the clock and coordinates I/O. It stores two input matrices in registers and includes a control unit and feeder module to schedule data through the array. The documentation claims over 99.8 million operations per second in a streamed processing pattern, though no silicon measurements are reported.

This project implements an AXI-Stream matrix-vector multiplier with a UART interface for host communication. It exposes only RX and TX pins, so all configuration and data transfer happen over the serial link. It requires an external USB-FTDI adapter for UART communication. The on-chip documentation is essentially absent, with all detail deferred to an external GitHub repository, so the internal architecture and performance cannot be assessed from the provided text.

This design is a crypto accelerator that performs AES encryption and decryption. It communicates over an SPI-style interface with sclk, chip select, and mosi/miso pins, and it also has a QSPI memory interface with four data lines plus clock and chip select for external memory. The documentation does not specify the required external hardware beyond the memory interface, and the testing instructions are limited to wiring it up. The provided documentation is extremely sparse and gives no detail on key handling, modes, or throughput.

This design is a copy of the VGA playground Stripes example, modified so the stripe pattern toggles direction back and forth. It outputs standard Tiny VGA signals and is tested in the same way as the original Stripes example. It requires only a VGA Pmod and a monitor. The documentation is very brief and does not explain the toggle behavior or any parameters beyond the title.

This design lets a user play an ocarina-style instrument on screen using a gamepad, with the notes rendered as VGA graphics and sound produced through a PWM audio output. It uses three gamepad pins for the controller and outputs Tiny VGA signals plus audio on a bidirectional pin. It requires a VGA Pmod, an audio Pmod, and a gamepad Pmod with a gamepad. The documentation is minimal and does not describe the note mapping, visual feedback, or any limitations.

This design outputs a pleasant-looking scene to a VGA display, described only as using XOR, addition, and magic in its generation logic. It is used by plugging in a TinyVGA Pmod, connecting a monitor, and applying a reset signal. The only external hardware required is the TinyVGA Pmod. The documentation is very thin and does not describe the scene content or the rendering technique in any meaningful detail.
